entities.name: Givi Amilakhvari
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Givi Amilakhvari (1689–1754) was a preeminent Georgian nobleman, or *tavadi*, whose tumultuous career defined much of eastern Georgia's political landscape during the first half of the 18th century. Operating amidst the geopolitical maelstrom of the Caucasus, he became a pivotal figure in Kartli's desperate struggle for survival against the encroaching Ottoman and Safavid (later Afsharid) empires. His significance lies in his relentless, albeit often shifting, efforts to preserve the autonomy of his native kingdom of Kartli, navigating a complex web of alliances and betrayals that characterized the region's early modern history.

Amilakhvari's political life was a continuous series of military campaigns and diplomatic maneuvers. Initially a loyal subject, he rose to prominence as a military commander under King Vakhtang VI, leading forces against Ottoman incursions in the 1720s. Following the Ottoman occupation of Kartli, he famously defected to the Safavid side in 1734, receiving Persian recognition as a *naib* (governor) and fighting against the Ottomans. However, perceiving the growing Persian (Afsharid) threat under Nader Shah, Amilakhvari initiated a major anti-Persian rebellion in 1740, rallying other Georgian nobles and mountain tribes. His forces engaged in numerous skirmishes and battles across Kartli and Kakheti, including the siege of Gori in 1744, earning him a reputation as a cunning and resilient guerrilla leader.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Givi Amilakhvari's persistent, decades-long struggle against both Ottoman and Persian imperial powers significantly prolonged the autonomy of the Kingdom of Kartli, preventing its immediate absorption. His actions diverted imperial attention, indirectly facilitating the later unification of Georgian kingdoms under Erekle II.
